title: John Donne
hook: a poet-dean: no man is an island; any man's death diminishes me

segments.voice: Yesterday, George Herbert, and a soul that finally sat down to eat. Your line was love bade me welcome.

A man lies sick in bed in London, too ill to get up. Through the window comes a church bell, tolling slowly, the way a passing bell rang when someone in the parish was dying. He doesn't know who it's for. Instead of finding out, he turns the thought over, and writes. That sick man had once written daring love poems, then became a priest and the dean of St Paul's Cathedral in London. Out of that sickbed came a few lines that still turn up far from any church.

John Donne wrote his Devotions during a serious illness: meditations, prayers and arguments with himself about sickness, death and God. In one, he hears the bell and wonders whether it's tolling for someone he doesn't know, or, if he's sicker than he thinks, for himself. Then comes this, in modern spelling: "No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main". The main is the mainland. A little later: "any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind". And he ends: "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee." Donne uses man the way his century did, for every human being, which is why today's line says no one. His point is sharper than a pleasant feeling of connection. In his view, a stranger's death actually takes something from each of us, because we're part of the same body of humankind. Some readers hear Paul behind it. Paul describes the church as one body with many parts, in the King James Bible: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it." Donne stretched that body wide. Every bell, every funeral, every name in the news is, in his picture, a clod of earth washed away by the sea.

Start with something close, the chair under you, your clothes, the last thing you ate, and ask quietly: who grew it, sewed it, drove it here? Let the faces you'll never meet come to mind, and follow one thread back to the field, the factory, the ship, feeling yourself a piece of the continent. If you pray, hold them all before God for a moment; if you don't, rest in being part of the main.
John Donne. A poet who became a priest and dean of St Paul's, who wrote from a sickbed that no one is an island, and that the tolling bell tolls for each of us.
Your line: no one is an island. The bell is never only for a stranger. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

notes: Audit: the bell in Meditation 17 is a passing bell, tolled for someone dying ('this bell tolling softly for another'), not only after a death; hook and fork corrected.
Claims rule: no dates or ages. Donne's earlier love poems and his role as dean of St Paul's come from the index hook ('poet-dean') and standard biography; confirm.
Quotations from Meditation 17 are given in the common modernized spelling (the 1624 text reads 'No man is an Iland, intire of it selfe...'); confirm the modernized wording.
'The line that gave a novel its title' refers to Hemingway's For Whom the Bell Tolls (not named); confirm or cut.
